\begin{abstract}
An advertising platform can pace a daily budget by forecasting the cost of the
remaining impressions and choosing what share to keep. Does a neural forecast
improve this decision? We compare five neural predictors with seasonal-naive and
LightGBM forecasts on \res{data-campaigns} Criteo campaigns, using a fixed
impression-replay rule at three budget levels. The target is hourly spend in
Criteo's transformed cost units, not impression counts.

All five neural predictors capture more clicks than the seasonal-naive plan:
\res{nn-gain-min}--\res{nn-gain-max} additional percentage points of the
hindsight-reference click count. They spend \res{nn-spend-min}--\res{nn-spend-max}\%
more, with little change in clicks per unit of spend. Multiplying the naive
forecast by a validation-chosen scale recovers \res{sn-share-rho0.3}--\res{sn-share-rho0.7}\%
of TFT's gain. In a separate experiment that swaps daily totals and hourly
profiles, the TFT total accounts for \res{ex-tshare-min}--\res{ex-tshare-max}\%
of the improvement. An exploratory comparison at equal aggregate spend leaves
all five models \res{nn-above-min}--\res{nn-above-max} points above the naive
scaling curve; this does not identify which part of the forecast causes the
remaining gain. For the four forecasters in the original study, planning with
90th-percentile hourly forecasts loses \res{hedge-cost-min}--\res{hedge-cost-max}
points relative to median forecasts. Calibration recovers only part of that loss.

These findings cover \res{cfg-test-days} test days in a simulator that barely
penalizes early budget exhaustion. The intervals exclude training-seed
uncertainty. A small iPinYou comparison does not reproduce the policy ordering
and does not test neural predictors. The evidence supports a gain on Criteo,
not a general advantage across advertising markets.
\end{abstract}

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}

An advertiser's daily budget may run out before the day ends, or remain partly
unspent. Budget pacing controls how quickly the platform spends it
\cite{lee2013real,agarwal2014budget}. One approach is \emph{probabilistic
throttling}: the platform participates in each eligible auction with probability
$\alpha_t$, which it updates during the day
\cite{agarwal2014budget,xu2015smart,balseiro2017budget}.

A reactive controller adjusts this probability using past spend. A
proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller, for example, tracks the gap
between actual spend and a target schedule. A forecast-based rule instead
estimates how much the remaining impressions would cost. It divides the
remaining budget by that estimate to choose the participation rate. Forecasting
too much spend lowers participation and may leave budget unused.

We ask whether neural predictors improve this rule, and what information they
add. A spend forecast provides both a daily total and an hourly profile: the
share of the total assigned to each hour. A better total could help even if the
hourly profile adds little. We also test whether using an upper quantile,
rather than the median hourly forecast, protects against early exhaustion at
an acceptable cost in clicks.

The main study uses the public Criteo Attribution dataset
\cite{diemert2017attribution}. We compare the Temporal Fusion Transformer
(TFT), NHITS, PatchTST, a long short-term memory (LSTM) model and TiDE with
seasonal naive and LightGBM. The initial study tested TFT and NHITS; the other
three neural models were added later. TFT remains the reference for the
experiments that examine totals, profiles and feedback.

The paper contributes an hourly spend-forecasting and replay pipeline, a
comparison with forecast-free policies, and experiments that separate the
benefits of spending more from changes in clicks per unit of spend. We then
test forecast scaling, total--profile swaps, perfect remaining-spend knowledge,
and conservative planning. A generated audience environment and a small
iPinYou study examine how much of the pattern carries beyond Criteo.

These are empirical comparisons of established models and pacing rules, not a
new architecture or a theoretical guarantee. The main results use
\res{cfg-test-days} test days. Follow-up experiments were designed after those
results were known; their timing and decision rules are disclosed in
Section~\ref{sec:protocol} and the accompanying protocol. All reported
measurements come from saved results files. Code, protocol and results files
will be released.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Pacing rules.} Lee et al.~\cite{lee2013real} study bidding with smooth
budget delivery. Agarwal et al.~\cite{agarwal2014budget} use supply patterns to
pace campaigns at LinkedIn. Smart pacing~\cite{xu2015smart} learns participation
rates for different segments. Dai et al.~\cite{dai2023percentile} control
probabilistic throttling with dual multipliers and report online tests on
Taobao. Balseiro et al.~\cite{balseiro2017budget} compare budget-management
strategies in equilibrium, while Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2014optimal} study
optimal bidding under budget constraints.

Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2016feedback} use feedback to adjust bids toward
winning-rate and cost-per-click targets. Our PID baseline adjusts participation
instead of bid prices. Chen's practical guide~\cite{chen2025practical} covers
throttling, PID, model-predictive control and dual online-gradient methods. It
notes that a PID controller cannot repair a misspecified target merely by
tracking it, and discusses updating the remaining-supply forecast.

\textbf{Forecasts and decisions.} Shekhar and Howard~\cite{shekhar2026decision}
calibrate uncertainty according to its effect on pacing decisions. Their
experiments use replays calibrated from Criteo Uplift and KuaiRand, rather than
the Criteo Attribution replay used here. They find that the lowest forecast
error need not give the smallest pacing-specific uncertainty radius. We study
a different question: how much changing the forecast improves clicks under a
fixed throttling rule.

TFT~\cite{lim2021temporal} combines recurrent encoding, variable selection and
attention. NHITS~\cite{challu2023nhits} uses multi-rate sampling and hierarchical
interpolation. We use their \texttt{neuralforecast} implementations, along with
the library's PatchTST~\cite{nie2023patchtst}, LSTM~\cite{hochreiter1997lstm} and
TiDE~\cite{das2023tide} models~\cite{olivares2022neuralforecast}.
LightGBM~\cite{ke2017lightgbm} provides a non-neural learned baseline. This study
evaluates these models as forecasting tools; it does not propose changes to
their architectures.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Pacing Setup}\label{sec:setup}

\textbf{What is forecast.} The target is the sum of logged impression costs in
each campaign-hour. We call this \emph{spend demand}: the cost of keeping all
impressions in that part of the log, before applying our throttle. It is neither
an impression count nor a forecast of spend after pacing. Criteo transforms
the costs, so spend and budget are measured in transformed cost units, not
currency.

\textbf{Episodes and budgets.} One episode is a campaign-day of 24 hours. The
budget is $B=\rho\bar D_c$, where $\bar D_c$ is campaign $c$'s mean daily
\emph{training} spend. We use $\rho\in\{0.3,0.5,0.7\}$, called the tight,
medium and loose budgets. Logged daily spend demand exceeds the budget in
\res{binding-rho0.3}\%, \res{binding-rho0.5}\% and
\res{binding-rho0.7}\% of test episodes, respectively.

\textbf{Replay.} At the start of hour $h$, the policy sets a retention
probability $\alpha_h\in[0,1]$. Each logged impression is kept independently
with that probability. Within the hour, kept impressions contribute their
logged cost, click and attributed conversion in chronological order, stopping
before the next kept impression would exceed the remaining budget. The same
uniform random draws are used for each policy, campaign, hour and replay seed.

This is a replay of \emph{won impressions}, not a simulation of all auctions.
The original bidder's choices already shaped the log. We assume that keeping
fewer impressions does not change their prices or outcomes. The log cannot
verify this counterfactual, and the replay does not model bid-price changes or
competitors' responses.

\textbf{Policies.} Let $S_h$ be cumulative spend before hour $h$ and
$R_h=B-S_h$ the remaining budget.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{No pacing}: keep every impression that fits the remaining budget
        ($\alpha_h=1$).
  \item \emph{Even pacing}: start at $\alpha_0=\min(1,B/\bar D_c)$ and adjust
        the previous rate multiplicatively toward spending $R_h/(24-h)$ per
        remaining hour.
  \item \emph{PID}: use the normalized spending gap $e_h=(Bh/24-S_h)/B$ to set
        $\alpha_h=\alpha_0+K_pe_h+K_i\sum_{j\leq h}e_j+K_d(e_h-e_{h-1})$.
        The replay clips the rate to $[0,1]$. Gains are grid-searched on
        validation days separately for each budget level.
  \item \emph{Forecast throttle}: forecast hourly spend demand for the rest of
        the day and set
        \begin{equation}
          \alpha_h = \min\Bigl(1,\; R_h \big/ \textstyle\sum_{j=h}^{23} \hat{y}^{(q)}_j\Bigr),
          \qquad q \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}.
          \label{eq:throttle}
        \end{equation}
        Here $\hat y_j^{(q)}$ is an hourly quantile forecast issued at the
        start of hour $h$. The plan is updated every hour.
  \item \emph{Hindsight constant}: use the fixed rate $\alpha=\min(1,B/D)$,
        where $D$ is the day's logged spend demand. This reference supplies
        the denominator of our click ratio. It is not an upper bound: a
        time-varying policy can capture more clicks.
\end{itemize}
Using a higher $q$ usually increases the denominator in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:throttle}, reducing participation. We call this \emph{hedging}
against early budget exhaustion. The denominator sums hourly quantiles; it is
not generally the same quantile of total remaining spend demand.

\textbf{Scaling and fixed plans.} The scaled-naive policy multiplies the
median-forecast denominator by $s$. A smaller $s$ raises participation. One
scale per budget level is selected on validation days from 25 values between
0.50 and 1.10. For total--profile swaps, we hold the day-start forecast fixed.
Its sum supplies the daily total and its normalized hourly values supply the
profile. We take these two components from either TFT or seasonal naive. An
\emph{oracle forecast} replaces the predicted total or remaining spend demand
with its actual logged value; the throttling rule is unchanged.

\textbf{Calibrated hedging.} Instead of summing upper hourly quantiles, we
multiply the median plan by a factor $f_q(h)$. The factor is the empirical
$q$-quantile of actual remaining spend demand divided by the median plan, for
that hour. Calibration uses all campaigns on earlier test days only. The
comparison therefore covers the last \res{ph-test-days-causal} test days.
A separate cross-fitted variant uses factors from other campaigns, including
their same-day data; it is not a deployable causal forecast.

\textbf{Feedback and dual-gradient control.} We add a PID correction to the
forecast rate, first using a spending schedule from the day-start forecast,
then using the previous hour's updated plan. Feedback gains are tuned with
seasonal naive and transferred unchanged to TFT and NHITS. We also test a
reactive dual-gradient rule, a throttling version of dual-gradient bid
pacing~\cite{balseiro2019learning}, $\alpha_h=\min(1,1/(1+\mu_h))$. Each hour its
nonnegative multiplier increases when spend exceeds an hourly target and
decreases when spend falls short. Targets are either flat ($B/24$) or based on
the campaign's training-hour profile. Step sizes are chosen on validation days.

\section{Forecasting Models}

Each forecast predicts the next 24 hours of campaign spend demand, using only
information available before its issue hour. We issue forecasts every hour
without refitting the models. All forecasters output quantiles
$\{0.1,0.5,0.7,0.9\}$; pacing uses the hours remaining in the current day.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Seasonal naive}: take empirical quantiles of spend in the same
        hour on the previous seven days. At $q=0.5$, this is their median.
  \item \emph{LightGBM}: fit one quantile-regression model per quantile, with
        forecast step as an input. Other inputs are spend lags, rolling
        statistics, calendar phase and campaign statistics computed on training
        hours. Spend is normalized by the campaign's training mean.
  \item \emph{TFT} and \emph{NHITS}: take \res{cfg-lookback} hours of past
        data. Both use multi-quantile loss and robust scaling. Inputs include spend,
        past impressions and clicks, known calendar phase and training-derived
        campaign statistics.
  \item \emph{PatchTST}, \emph{LSTM} and \emph{TiDE}: add a patch-based
        transformer, a recurrent model and a dense encoder--decoder. They use
        the same training procedure, with architecture-specific settings fixed
        before their runs. LSTM and TiDE use the covariates above. PatchTST
        uses only past spend.
\end{itemize}
Learned models are fitted on training days and early-stopped using validation
days. Each neural model has \res{n-nn-seeds} training seeds; LightGBM has one
run. Hyperparameters are listed in the protocol and code. The original
comparison covers TFT, NHITS and the two non-neural forecasters. PatchTST,
LSTM and TiDE were added under protocol entry 21 and evaluated for median-plan
pacing. The hedging and feedback experiments were not repeated for these
three additions.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Experimental Protocol}

\begin{table}[tb]
  \caption{Original four forecasters: mean test accuracy ($\pm$ training-seed SD). MASE$_h$ is MASE at step $h$; Cov.\ is 80\% prediction-interval coverage. Time includes fitting and forecasting.}
  \label{tab:forecast}
  \small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../results/tables/forecast_main.tex}}
\end{table}

\textbf{Data and splits.} The Criteo dataset contains \res{data-impressions}
impressions from \res{data-campaigns-total} campaigns over \res{cfg-n-hours}
hours. We use the first \res{cfg-use-days} complete days and discard the last
\res{cfg-discard-hours} hours. Training uses \res{cfg-train-days} days,
validation the next \res{cfg-val-days}, and testing the last
\res{cfg-test-days}. Day boundaries are relative to the dataset start, not
local midnight. The dataset license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

We retain campaigns with nonzero spend in at least \res{cfg-min-active}\% of
training hours. This gives \res{data-campaigns} campaigns, representing
\res{data-spend-share}\% of dataset spend, and \res{data-test-episodes}
test campaign-days. Each episode has \res{n-replay-seeds} replay seeds. The
selection rule uses training hours, but its threshold was chosen after a
descriptive profile of the whole dataset, including test hours.

\textbf{Forecast metrics.} Mean absolute scaled error
(MASE)~\cite{hyndman2006another} divides forecast error by the same campaign's
training error from a lag-24 forecast. A value below one beats that training
scale; it does not necessarily beat the seasonal-naive model on the test set.
We also measure pinball loss~\cite{koenker1978regression}, coverage of the
nominal 80\% prediction interval, and quantile crossings. Scaled pinball loss
(sPL) divides pinball loss by mean training hourly spend. Reported fitting and
forecasting times use one RTX 3070 Ti for neural models and an Apple M4 CPU for
LightGBM; they are not hardware-matched speed comparisons.

\textbf{Pacing metrics.} The primary metric is total clicks divided by the
hindsight constant-rate reference's total clicks, pooled over episodes and
seeds. A gain of one point means one percentage point of this ratio, or 1\%
of the reference click count. It is not a relative percentage gain over the
compared policy. We also report attributed-conversion ratios, budget utilization
(BUR, spend divided by budget), early depletion before hour
\res{cfg-early-hour}, and the pacing volatility index (PVI, the root-mean-square
hourly change in $\alpha_h$). Spend changes and changes in clicks per unit of
spend are relative percentages.

\textbf{Uncertainty.} Confidence intervals (CIs) use
\res{n-bootstrap} campaign-bootstrap resamples, with paired differences
between policies. The original \res{n-comparisons} paired comparisons use
Wilcoxon signed-rank tests~\cite{wilcoxon1945individual} with Holm
correction~\cite{holm1979simple}. These tests use the
\res{cmp-n-campaigns} campaigns with positive reference clicks; other Criteo
analyses use all \res{data-campaigns}. Training seeds are pooled within
campaigns. Thus the intervals and tests condition on the saved trained models
and do not include training-seed uncertainty. We report seed variation
separately. We did not compute confidence intervals for MASE differences.

\textbf{Protocol and deviations.}\label{sec:protocol} A written protocol
preceded the main evaluation, but test data were not entirely unseen. Besides
the full-dataset profile, smoke tests inspected test-origin accuracy for
seasonal naive, LightGBM and a short TFT run, and replayed ten campaigns' test
days. The log reports no hyperparameter change in response to those test
results. The PID search grid was widened using validation results. Failed GPU
runs wrote no forecasts and were retried. At the final neural forecast origin,
the preceding forecast was shifted by one hour because a full future window
was unavailable.

The decomposition, scaling, hedging calibration, feedback, oracle and subgroup
analyses were not planned before the main results were seen. New simulations
were logged before execution, with decision rules where specified. The spend
and subgroup analyses only reread saved episodes and were logged afterward.
The original matched-spend comparison had no decision rule. Entry 21 later
set rules before training the three additional neural models; this does not
make the overall research sequence a single pre-registered test. The corrected
dual-gradient variant was also added after its first results were seen.

Two protocol metrics are not reported here: hourly spend deviation from the
reference profile, retained in \texttt{pacing\_summary.csv}, and validation-split
forecast metrics. The protocol originally specified a seven-day mean for
seasonal naive; the implementation used empirical quantiles, hence the median
at $q=0.5$. An independent rerun rebuilt the data, retuned PID, regenerated
seasonal-naive and LightGBM forecasts, and reproduced the pacing summary. It
reused the neural forecasts with matching checksums; neural training was not
independently repeated.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Results}

\subsection{Forecast accuracy}
In the original comparison, mean MASE is lowest for TFT
(\res{fc-tft-mase}), followed by NHITS (\res{fc-nhits-mase}), LightGBM
(\res{fc-lightgbm-mase}) and seasonal naive (\res{fc-naive-mase}); see
Table~\ref{tab:forecast}. All four are below the in-sample lag-24 scale.
The later five-model comparison is shown in Table~\ref{tab:neural}.

The mean ranking does not hold for every campaign. Median campaign MASE is
\res{fc-tft-medmase} for TFT, \res{fc-nhits-medmase} for NHITS and
\res{fc-lightgbm-medmase} for LightGBM. TFT has lower error than LightGBM in
\res{win-tft-lightgbm}\% of campaigns, and NHITS in
\res{win-nhits-lightgbm}\%. These differences are descriptive, without paired
accuracy CIs. Separately, the prediction intervals cover too few outcomes:
the nominal 80\% interval covers \res{fc-tft-cov80}\% for TFT and
\res{fc-naive-cov80}\% for seasonal naive. Prediction-interval coverage and
uncertainty about average MASE differences are different questions.

\subsection{Pacing outcomes}\label{sec:pacing}
Median-plan TFT and NHITS capture \res{gain-even-min}--\res{gain-even-max}
points more clicks than even pacing and \res{gain-pid-min}--\res{gain-pid-max}
points more than tuned PID (Table~\ref{tab:pacing}). Seasonal naive already
adds \res{gain-naive-even-min}--\res{gain-naive-even-max} points over even
pacing; the two neural models add \res{nn-naive-min}--\res{nn-naive-max}
points beyond that. All \res{cmp-nn-baselines-sig} of
\res{cmp-nn-baselines-total} paired neural-versus-even-or-PID comparisons are
significant after Holm correction (largest adjusted $p=\res{cmp-nn-baselines-pmax}$).
These tests condition on the trained models and do not include the later
PatchTST, LSTM and TiDE runs.

TFT and NHITS also change their participation rates less sharply than PID.
Their PVI is \res{fc-pvi-min}--\res{fc-pvi-max}, versus
\res{pid-pvi-min}--\res{pid-pvi-max} for PID. Their early-depletion rate is
\res{fc-early-min}--\res{fc-early-max}\%, versus
\res{pid-early-min}--\res{pid-early-max}\%. These are replay measurements,
not evidence of stability in a live auction system.

\textbf{TFT and NHITS are close, not proven equivalent.} Their median-plan
click ratios differ by at most \res{tft-nhits-diff-max} points. Across training
seeds, the SD reaches \res{nhits-seed-sd-max} points for NHITS and
\res{tft-seed-sd-max} for TFT. Only \res{cmp-tft-nhits-sig} of
\res{cmp-tft-nhits-total} paired comparisons is significant. We have neither
seed-aware inference nor an equivalence test, so we do not claim identical
performance. Their gains over LightGBM span \res{nn-lgb-min}--\res{nn-lgb-max}
points; the smallest gain is below NHITS's seed SD.

In an exploratory split by training-period campaign size and volatility, TFT's
gain over seasonal naive is positive in all \res{grp-n-cells} group-and-budget
cells (\res{grp-gain-min} to \res{grp-gain-max} points). Gains are larger in
the most volatile third at the two tighter budgets, but the intervals overlap
and are not corrected for multiple comparisons.

\begin{table}[tb]
  \caption{Five-model extension. MASE averages campaigns and training seeds. Click gains and distances above the spend-matched naive curve are in reference-click points.}
  \label{tab:neural}
  \small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../results/tables/neural.tex}}
\end{table}

\textbf{All five tested neural models beat seasonal naive on Criteo.}
Table~\ref{tab:neural} adds PatchTST, LSTM and TiDE to the comparison.
Seasonal-naive MASE is \res{nn-mase-naive}, and LightGBM MASE is
\res{nn-mase-lightgbm}. All \res{nn-n-beat} of \res{nn-n-models} neural
models gain \res{nn-gain-min}--\res{nn-gain-max} click-ratio points over
seasonal naive across the three budgets, with every gain CI above zero.
All \res{nn-n-edge} also lie above the spend-matched scaling curve described
below, by \res{nn-above-min}--\res{nn-above-max} points.

Entry 21 required at least four of five models to show each finding at two of
three budgets. Both findings meet that rule, whose label is
``\res{nn-beat-verdict}.'' Here the label describes the tested architectures
on these Criteo logs, not all neural predictors or other datasets. The
matched-spend method itself originated as an exploratory analysis.

The models spend \res{nn-spend-min}--\res{nn-spend-max}\% more than seasonal
naive. Changes in clicks per unit of spend range from \res{nn-eff-min}\% to
\res{nn-eff-max}\%; these point estimates are small but do not establish
equivalence in efficiency. Ranking the five models by mean MASE gives the
reverse of their ranking by mean click gain (Spearman correlation
\res{nn-spearman}). This is descriptive: five models are too few to establish
a general relationship, and TFT and NHITS have nearly equal mean gains.
PatchTST remains competitive despite using no extra covariates.

\subsection{Where the gain comes from}\label{sec:where}
\begin{table}[tb]
  \caption{Median-plan comparisons. Click gains are reference-click points with 95\% campaign-bootstrap CIs; spend and efficiency columns are relative percentage changes.}
  \label{tab:decomp}
  \small\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
  \resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{../results/tables/decomp.tex}}
\end{table}

\textbf{More spend, with little change in efficiency.} TFT spends
\res{se-tft-naive-spend-min}--\res{se-tft-naive-spend-max}\% more than
seasonal naive (Table~\ref{tab:decomp}). Clicks per unit of spend change by
\res{se-tft-naive-eff-min}\% to \res{se-tft-naive-eff-max}\%, with CIs
including zero at \res{se-tft-naive-eff-ci0} of three budgets. NHITS shows
a similar pattern. Thus the extra clicks over this baseline mainly accompany
more budget spent, rather than a measured improvement in clicks per unit of
spend.

The comparison with PID differs. TFT's relative spend change is
\res{se-tft-pid-spend-min}\% to \res{se-tft-pid-spend-max}\%, while clicks
per unit of spend rise by \res{se-tft-pid-eff-min}--\res{se-tft-pid-eff-max}\%.
The efficiency CIs are above zero at all three budgets. This describes where
the click gain appears; it does not identify a causal auction-selection
mechanism.

\textbf{Scaling the naive forecast.} Lowering the forecast denominator makes
the throttle keep more impressions. We select scales of
\res{sn-scale-rho0.3}, \res{sn-scale-rho0.5} and \res{sn-scale-rho0.7} on
validation days for the tight, medium and loose budgets. None is at the grid
edge. On test days, this captures \res{sn-share-rho0.3}\%,
\res{sn-share-rho0.5}\% and \res{sn-share-rho0.7}\% of TFT's gain over
unscaled seasonal naive. The scaled plan also spends more, but its clicks per
unit of spend fall (Table~\ref{tab:decomp}).

TFT retains a positive gain over the scaled plan at the tight and medium
budgets. At the loose budget, the difference is \res{sn-gap-rho0.7} points
with CI \res{sn-gap-ci-rho0.7}, so there is no clear separation. By entry 19's
rule, ``an edge beyond one scale remains''; scaling does not explain almost
all of the gain at every budget. This is one global scale per budget level,
not a separate correction for each campaign or day.

\begin{table*}[t]
  \caption{Click-ratio gains in points; brackets give 95\% campaign-bootstrap CIs. Swaps hold day-start plans fixed; the oracle updates remaining spend each hour.}
  \label{tab:swaps}
  \centering\small
  \begin{tabular}{lccc}
    \toprule
    Comparison & Tight ($\rho=0.3$) & Medium ($\rho=0.5$) & Loose ($\rho=0.7$) \\
    \midrule
    \multicolumn{4}{l}{Fixed plan minus fixed seasonal-naive plan} \\
    TFT total, TFT profile & \res{ex-g-rho0.3} & \res{ex-g-rho0.5} & \res{ex-g-rho0.7} \\
    TFT total, naive profile & \res{ex-t-rho0.3} \res{ex-t-ci-rho0.3} & \res{ex-t-rho0.5} \res{ex-t-ci-rho0.5} & \res{ex-t-rho0.7} \res{ex-t-ci-rho0.7} \\
    Naive total, TFT profile & \res{ex-s-rho0.3} \res{ex-s-ci-rho0.3} & \res{ex-s-rho0.5} \res{ex-s-ci-rho0.5} & \res{ex-s-rho0.7} \res{ex-s-ci-rho0.7} \\
    \midrule
    Oracle remaining spend $-$ TFT & \res{ex-head-rho0.3} \res{ex-head-ci-rho0.3} & \res{ex-head-rho0.5} \res{ex-head-ci-rho0.5} & \res{ex-head-rho0.7} \res{ex-head-ci-rho0.7} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table*}

\textbf{Swapping the daily total and hourly profile.} To separate these two
parts of the forecast, we build fixed plans from the forecasts issued at the
start of the day. We replace either the naive plan's daily spend total or its
hourly shares with TFT's, leaving the other component unchanged
(Table~\ref{tab:swaps}). These are spend totals and spend shares, not traffic
counts or impression-arrival profiles.

Replacing only the total captures \res{ex-tshare-min}--\res{ex-tshare-max}\%
of the gain from replacing both components. Replacing only the profile adds
less, but its CI is above zero at the medium and loose budgets. The protocol
therefore attributes the gain to the total at the tight budget and reports a
partial result at the other two. The two component gains need not sum to the
combined gain. Updating forecasts hourly adds a further
\res{ex-replan-min}--\res{ex-replan-max} points for TFT relative to its fixed
day-start plan. This experiment was run for TFT, not all five neural models.

\textbf{Perfect knowledge under the same rule.} Replacing TFT's forecasts
with actual remaining logged spend demand adds
\res{ex-head-min}--\res{ex-head-max} points (Table~\ref{tab:swaps}). The
protocol calls this moderate headroom. The oracle is an information benchmark
for this particular throttle, not a proven upper bound on clicks or on what
another pacing rule could achieve. Its information still concerns the stream
selected by the original logging policy.

\textbf{Matching aggregate spend (exploratory).} We use the 25 naive scales
to trace a curve of total spend against total clicks. For each model, we
linearly interpolate this curve at that model's aggregate spend. The five
neural models lie \res{nn-above-min}--\res{nn-above-max} click-ratio points
above it, with every CI above zero (Table~\ref{tab:neural}). LightGBM is also
above the curve at the tight budget (\res{fr-lgb-rho0.3} points,
CI \res{fr-lgb-ci-rho0.3}); its medium- and loose-budget intervals include zero.

The comparison matches overall spend, not spend within every campaign-day.
It shows that one global rescaling does not reproduce the neural outcomes.
It cannot distinguish campaign-specific total predictions, hourly allocation
and hourly re-planning, or establish that the models select intrinsically
better auctions. The analysis was introduced after the scaling results and
had no initial decision rule. Its intervals also exclude training-seed
uncertainty.

\textbf{Another reactive baseline.} The flat-target dual-gradient rule has
a click-ratio difference of \res{dg-flat-pid-min} to
\res{dg-flat-pid-max} points relative to tuned PID. TFT and scaled naive
both beat it, meeting entry 20's rule that ``the forecast advantage survives
a tuned dual-gradient pacer.'' A profile-target variant under-spends. After
seeing that result, we normalized its hourly error by $B/24$ instead of the
hour-specific target. TFT still leads the corrected variant by
\res{dg-tft-profn-min}--\res{dg-tft-profn-max} points. PID remains the
strongest reactive rule tested here; this does not rule out better controller
designs or tuning.

\subsection{Hedging}\label{sec:hedge}
\begin{figure}[tb]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig_tradeoff_rho0.5.pdf}
  \Description{At the medium budget, higher planning quantiles reduce both budget utilization and early depletion. The depletion axis is logarithmic.}
  \caption{Budget utilization versus early depletion at $\rho=0.5$. The depletion axis is logarithmic; lines connect $q=0.5,0.7,0.9$.}
  \label{fig:tradeoff}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Higher hourly quantiles leave more budget unspent.} Across the four
original forecasters, clicks fall as $q$ rises from 0.5 to 0.7 to 0.9 in all
\res{hedge-mono} of \res{hedge-mono-total} forecaster-and-budget combinations.
Moving from 0.5 to 0.9 costs \res{hedge-cost-min}--\res{hedge-cost-max}
click-ratio points. All \res{cmp-q09-baselines-neg} comparisons of 0.9 plans
with even pacing and PID favor those baselines; \res{cmp-q09-baselines-sig}
are significant after the original Holm correction.

The upper plans reduce early depletion to
\res{hedge-early-min}--\res{hedge-early-max}\% of episodes, but budget
utilization falls to \res{hedge-bur-min}--\res{hedge-bur-max}\%
(Figure~\ref{fig:tradeoff}). For TFT, the relative spend change versus even
pacing is \res{se-q09-spend-min}\% to \res{se-q09-spend-max}\%, despite
an increase in clicks per unit of spend. Fewer clicks accompany less budget
spent.

The objective here rewards clicks, without a separate penalty for exhausting
the budget early. At the loose budget, no pacing and tuned PID have nearly
equal click ratios (\res{nopacing-rho0.7-click} and
\res{pid-rho0.7-click}). Thus the observed cost of hedging partly reflects
this environment. It is not evidence that early exhaustion is unimportant to
advertisers.

\textbf{Hourly coverage does not determine total coverage.} A sum of hourly
quantiles is not generally the corresponding quantile of the remaining-day
total. We measure this difference rather than assume a particular dependence
between hourly errors. TFT's hourly 90th-percentile forecasts cover
\res{hc-hourly90-tft}\% of outcomes. Across the four forecasters, the summed
90\% plans cover \res{hc-cov90-min}--\res{hc-cov90-max}\% of actual
remaining spend totals at the evaluated origins, more than the nominal 90\%.
The summed plans are \res{hc-fac-sum-min}--\res{hc-fac-sum-max} times their
median plans. A diagnostic fitted to those test outcomes gives smaller
factors, \res{hc-fac-cal-min}--\res{hc-fac-cal-max}, for 90\% coverage.
These diagnostic factors are not a guarantee of future coverage.

\textbf{Calibration recovers part of the loss.} We next estimate factors
using earlier test days only and evaluate on the remaining
\res{ph-test-days-causal} days. At $q=0.9$, TFT recovers
\res{ch-rec-rho0.3}\%, \res{ch-rec-rho0.5}\% and
\res{ch-rec-rho0.7}\% of its summed-plan loss at the tight, medium and loose
budgets. Each improvement CI is above zero, but the recovery falls below
the protocol's one-third threshold. The rule therefore gives a partial
verdict, not that calibration fails entirely or explains most of the cost.

Calibration at $q=0.7$ recovers more of the loss, but TFT's calibrated-minus-median
differences remain negative: \res{ch70-resid-rho0.3},
\res{ch70-resid-rho0.5} and \res{ch70-resid-rho0.7} points. For seasonal
naive, calibrated 0.9 plans are worse than summed plans. The cross-fitted
variant is no better for TFT at 0.9 and is not an upper bound on clicks.
These results do not establish how much loss a different calibration method
could recover.

The objective also matters. No pacing captures
\res{nopacing-conv-min}--\res{nopacing-conv-max} points more attributed
conversions than the hindsight reference while capturing fewer clicks.
The policy ordering for clicks need not be the ordering for attributed
conversions; neither measures causal conversion lift.

\subsection{Adding feedback}\label{sec:fb}
\begin{table*}[t]
  \caption{Feedback comparisons in click-ratio points (95\% campaign-bootstrap CIs). Each block uses its own validation-tuned gains and scaled-naive baseline.}
  \label{tab:feedback}
  \centering\small
  \begin{tabular}{lccc}
    \toprule
    Comparison & Tight ($\rho=0.3$) & Medium ($\rho=0.5$) & Loose ($\rho=0.7$) \\
    \midrule
    \multicolumn{4}{l}{Feedback tracks the day-start plan} \\
    TFT with $-$ without feedback & \res{fb-tft-rho0.3} \res{fb-tft-ci-rho0.3} & \res{fb-tft-rho0.5} \res{fb-tft-ci-rho0.5} & \res{fb-tft-rho0.7} \res{fb-tft-ci-rho0.7} \\
    TFT $-$ scaled naive, both with feedback & \res{fb-tft-vs-scaled-rho0.3} \res{fb-tft-vs-scaled-ci-rho0.3} & \res{fb-tft-vs-scaled-rho0.5} \res{fb-tft-vs-scaled-ci-rho0.5} & \res{fb-tft-vs-scaled-rho0.7} \res{fb-tft-vs-scaled-ci-rho0.7} \\
    \midrule
    \multicolumn{4}{l}{Feedback tracks the previous hour's plan} \\
    TFT with $-$ without feedback & \res{fb2-tft-rho0.3} \res{fb2-tft-ci-rho0.3} & \res{fb2-tft-rho0.5} \res{fb2-tft-ci-rho0.5} & \res{fb2-tft-rho0.7} \res{fb2-tft-ci-rho0.7} \\
    TFT $-$ scaled naive, both with feedback & \res{fb2-tft-vs-scaled-rho0.3} \res{fb2-tft-vs-scaled-ci-rho0.3} & \res{fb2-tft-vs-scaled-rho0.5} \res{fb2-tft-vs-scaled-ci-rho0.5} & \res{fb2-tft-vs-scaled-rho0.7} \res{fb2-tft-vs-scaled-ci-rho0.7} \\
    \bottomrule
  \end{tabular}
\end{table*}

Feedback on the day-start plan helps TFT at the tight budget but lowers its
click ratio at the other two (Table~\ref{tab:feedback}). Tracking the previous
hour's updated plan does not give a clear TFT improvement at either tighter
budget and lowers clicks at the loose one. Entry 18 required a positive
feedback-gain CI at two of three budgets. Neither variant meets that rule:
the verdict is ``feedback does not help TFT.''

The same rule tests whether TFT with feedback beats scaled naive with
feedback. It does not do so at two of three budgets in either experiment,
giving ``the neural edge does not survive feedback.'' This is a verdict about
these feedback designs, not about all combinations of forecasting and control.
The day-start experiment uses the earlier scale-grid baseline; the hourly-plan
experiment uses the extended-grid baseline. They are not identical policy
comparisons.

The gains were tuned on seasonal naive, not on the neural forecasts. Some
selected gains reach the grid edge, and tuning uses only
\res{cfg-val-days} validation days. At the loose budget, seasonal-naive
feedback gains \res{fb-val-gain-loose} points on validation days but changes
test clicks by \res{fb-naive-rho0.7} points (CI
\res{fb-naive-ci-rho0.7}). Gain transfer and short-window tuning limit the
interpretation. We did not establish why feedback reduces TFT's clicks, so
we do not attribute the loss to jitter or overreaction.

\subsection{A second environment: a synthetic audience world}\label{sec:world}
We also use a generated opportunity stream, where the logging policy and
cost process are under our control. The generator creates \wres{users} users,
\wres{camps} campaigns and \wres{days} days, with planted daily and weekly
patterns and user churn (mean lifetime \wres{lifetime} days). The pacers know
the generated click probabilities, removing click-estimation error from this
comparison. This is a controlled pacing experiment, not a validated model
of a live advertising market.

Across \wres{worlds} worlds and \wres{costs} cost models, replaying the previous
seven days' opportunities gains \wres{replay-gain-min}--\wres{replay-gain-max}
points over reactive control. Here points are shares of a Lagrangian hindsight
value bound, not the Criteo click reference. Rescaling the replay to the true
expected traffic total adds only \wres{total-min}--\wres{total-max} points;
all intervals for that addition include zero. The combined gain over reactive
control is \wres{ahead-min}--\wres{ahead-max} points, with a CI above zero
only for time-of-day pricing.

Historical replay therefore captures nearly all of the observed forecasting
benefit in these worlds. This leaves little measured room for a more accurate
forecaster in that setting, rather than confirming a neural advantage.
The rhythms were built into the generator and daily totals vary less than in
the real logs. We do not use this result to establish cross-dataset
generalization of the Criteo findings.

\subsection{A second real dataset: iPinYou}\label{sec:ipinyou}
The iPinYou season-2 logs provide \res{ipy-impressions} million won impressions
from \res{ipy-advertisers} advertisers over seven days. We treat each advertiser
as a campaign: the first four days are training, one is validation, and two
are test days, giving \res{ipy-episodes} test episodes. Forecasts use the same
hour on the previous three days. We do not train or test neural predictors
on this dataset. Intervals resample test episodes rather than campaigns.

Entry 20 calls the replication consistent if scaled naive ranks at least as
high as naive, and naive at least as high as even pacing and PID, at two of
three budgets. This ordering holds at \res{ipy-consistent} levels, so the
descriptive verdict is ``inconsistent.'' Naive-minus-even click differences
are \res{ipy-naive-even-rho0.3}, \res{ipy-naive-even-rho0.5} and
\res{ipy-naive-even-rho0.7} points, with every CI including zero. No pacing
has the highest realistic-policy point estimate at the tight budget.

The oracle remaining-spend plan beats naive by
\res{ipy-oracle-naive-rho0.3} points (CI \res{ipy-oracle-naive-ci-rho0.3}),
\res{ipy-oracle-naive-rho0.5} (\res{ipy-oracle-naive-ci-rho0.5}) and
\res{ipy-oracle-naive-rho0.7} (\res{ipy-oracle-naive-ci-rho0.7}). This shows
an advantage for perfect logged-spend information under the same rule.
It does not show that a feasible learned model can obtain it. With few
advertisers, two test days, one tuning day and a selected scale at the grid
edge for the loose budget, the comparison neither reproduces the Criteo
ordering nor precisely establishes a contrary ordering.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Discussion}

\textbf{What the evidence supports.} All five tested neural models improve
clicks over seasonal naive on Criteo. Their extra clicks accompany more spend
and small changes in clicks per unit of spend. TFT's swap experiment points
mainly to its daily spend total rather than its hourly profile. A single
validation-chosen scale captures much of TFT's gain at the loose budget, but
less than half at the tight one. It is therefore useful to compare a neural
model with a scaled seasonal baseline, not only an unscaled one.

The remaining gain at matched aggregate spend is a result to explain, not a
mechanism already established. The comparison does not tell us whether it
comes from campaign-specific totals, hourly profiles or re-planning. Nor does
the five-model ranking establish that lowering MASE will reliably raise
clicks in a different setting. NHITS and TFT have close pacing outcomes,
while their recorded fitting-and-forecasting times differ
(\res{time-nhits}\,s and \res{time-tft}\,s on the same GPU setup).
That is a practical compute difference in these runs, not proof that the
architectures are interchangeable.

\textbf{Implications for this replay setting.} The median is the best of the
three planning quantiles tested for the original four forecasters. Lower
quantiles were not evaluated for pacing, so we do not claim that the median
is optimal. Better coverage of the remaining-spend total also does not
automatically give more clicks: a conservative plan can still leave budget
unspent. A system with explicit delivery or early-exhaustion penalties may
make a different trade-off.

Feedback should likewise be tested with the forecast and objective that will
actually be used. Transferring gains from seasonal naive did not consistently
improve TFT. This does not justify a blanket rule to add feedback only at
tight budgets. The small iPinYou comparison and the generated worlds also
do not establish where neural forecasting will work outside Criteo.

\textbf{Limits of the evidence.} The main evaluation spans
\res{cfg-test-days} days of one dataset. Campaign bootstrap intervals describe
variation across campaigns on those days, not uncertainty from a new test
period or retraining. All tests condition on saved neural forecasts;
LightGBM and seasonal naive have single runs. There are no paired accuracy
CIs or seed-aware pacing tests. In Table~\ref{tab:decomp}, CIs are shown
only for clicks; the TFT-versus-scaled-naive efficiency difference has no CI.

The replay uses only won impressions and transformed prices. It omits
competitive responses, price effects and a separate cost of early exhaustion.
The reference is not a ceiling and the oracle knows logged spend, not the
full auction market. Day boundaries are relative to the dataset start.
These restrictions limit both economic interpretation and deployment advice.

The main design was informed by a full-data profile and test smoke checks.
Later experiments reused the same test period after the main results were
known. Follow-up CIs are not a new Holm-corrected family of tests, and the
subgroup CIs are not corrected for multiple comparisons. Gains and scales
were tuned on only \res{cfg-val-days} validation days, with some controller
settings at search boundaries. The high PID volatility may indicate scope
for a better controller, but does not diagnose why feedback loses clicks.
More campaigns do not remove these time-period, tuning and design limits.

% ------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}

On Criteo, all five tested neural predictors capture more clicks than seasonal
naive under the same throttling rule. Most of TFT's improvement in the
day-start swap experiment comes from its daily spend total. Scaling the
seasonal baseline recovers \res{sn-share-rho0.3}--\res{sn-share-rho0.7}\%
of TFT's gain, depending on budget tightness. A smaller gain remains at
matched aggregate spend, but its cause is unresolved.

Upper-quantile plans leave more budget unspent in this click-focused replay.
Calibrating the total recovers part of the loss, and the tested feedback
designs do not consistently improve TFT. These findings are limited by a
short test period, fixed-model inference and the logging-policy assumptions.
The iPinYou study does not reproduce the policy ordering and tests no neural
models. The next empirical steps are seed-aware inference, longer
out-of-time evaluations on another real dataset, and a simulator that tests
price responses and explicit delivery constraints.
